Behavior needs its own denominator. A constraint-violation rate can count violating proposals among the proposals to which that constraint applies. The runtime should retain rejected proposals for this diagnosis without executing them. An executed-violation rate answers a different question about enforcement. Likewise, a stale-support rate can count decisions that treat a known superseded observation as current among decisions requiring current evidence. A historical reference to the r17 failure is not an error merely because the workspace is now at r18. The error is using that reference to assert a property of r18 without support. Fixtures and trace review must make the classification rule explicit.

Task acceptance provides the end-to-end measure. Its numerator is the number of trials meeting the stated acceptance standard within the limits; its denominator is all assigned trials. A reproducer pass is one observation within that standard, not an unrestricted claim that the patch is correct. Report unresolved trials and the reasons they stopped rather than excluding them from the denominator. The measurement contract in @tbl-vol3-context-evaluation keeps these different outcomes visible.

| Measurement              | What the evaluator records                                                                     | What the result cannot establish                           |
|:-------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|
| Required-field retention | Correct values and evidence scope at each specified compaction boundary                        | That the inventory includes every fact needed later        |
| Constraint compliance    | Violating proposals among applicable proposals, separately from executed violations            | That prompt text enforces an action boundary               |
| Current-evidence use     | Decisions using superseded support as current, among eligible decisions                        | That every old observation is irrelevant                   |
| Task acceptance          | Trials meeting the common evidence standard, including every assigned trial in the denominator | Correctness beyond that standard's coverage                |
| Request footprint        | Fully serialized input length, output reservation, and rejected oversized requests             | Lower total task cost or adequate information              |
| Resource use             | All calls, source reads, compaction, checks, and elapsed time charged to the cohort            | A benefit unless accepted outcomes justify the expenditure |

: **Context-policy measurement contract**: Representation checks, behavioral observations, and task outcomes answer different questions. Their denominators and coverage must remain explicit when comparing policies. {#tbl-vol3-context-evaluation tbl-colwidths="[21,43,36]"}

Compression is a representation ratio, not a quality metric. At a specified decision point, construct a reference request from the available history without compaction and a request from the evaluated policy. Count each complete serialized request with the same tokenizer, including its instructions, tool definitions, metadata, and framing. Define the request compression ratio as the reference token count divided by the policy token count. The reference may exceed the service limit; counting it does not imply that it can be submitted. A ratio above unity denotes a smaller request under this convention. Counting raw observations in the numerator but the whole prompt in the denominator would describe a different quantity and must not use the same interpretation.

The ratio also depends on which history is available. In a fixed-history probe, policies share that input, making their resulting request lengths directly comparable. In complete task trials, policies can generate different histories. A large compression ratio for one policy may reflect that it first produced more material to discard. Report absolute input counts and task expenditure alongside the ratio, including the cost of building summaries, obtaining fresh observations, and recovering omitted payloads. Context savings can otherwise hide work displaced into another call.

Evidence use is harder to establish than token presence. Attention weights and a model's quotation of an identifier do not by themselves show that the identifier caused a useful decision. A targeted intervention supplies stronger diagnostic evidence. Remove or alter a task-relevant field while keeping the rest of a controlled fixture fixed, repeat the next-decision probe, and compare the resulting behavior. The intervention tests dependence under those conditions, not a universal usefulness score for each token. The complete task trial remains necessary because a policy may compensate for the missing field by obtaining a fresh observation.

### Diagnosing a context-policy failure

The shared manifest supports a compact test of both compaction and invalidation. The probe requires the earlier failure to retain its historical scope, while any claim about the candidate must remain tied to the candidate actually checked. The example below describes an illustrative probe, not a measured deployment trace or a claimed advantage for a particular policy.

::: {#exmp-04-context-evidence-probe .callout-example title="A passing test without its version"}

**Scenario**: At r17, `test_waiter_notified_on_return` records that a connection becomes available while a waiter remains blocked. A candidate patch produces r18, and a check on r18 passes the reproducer under the recorded test configuration. Broader behavior remains untested. Before the next request, a compaction policy replaces these entries with “The waiter test passed; the repair is complete.” The task's API constraint and deployment prohibition remain in the request.

**Diagnosis**: A schema requiring a string-valued `test_status` can accept the summary, and a constraint-presence test can find both retained restrictions. Neither catches the promotion of a scoped observation into task completion. The evidence probe checks the candidate and test identities, the reproducer's scope, and the unresolved acceptance obligations. A subsequent controlled variant changes a relevant test or source input after the passing run. The next decision should recognize that the earlier pass does not establish the changed candidate's behavior and obtain the required current evidence before making that claim. An unrelated file change supplies a contrasting variant in which the evaluator must not demand indiscriminate invalidation.

**Systems lesson**: The policy must preserve relationships, not only field names. A result needs the artifact and conditions it describes, and the next action must respect the limits of that result. The probe locates information loss; repeated task trials determine whether the repair policy uses the preserved distinctions effectively.

:::

The same method can test omission rather than overstatement. If compaction removes the exact test identifier but retains a raw-log handle, the next request no longer contains that identifier. Whether the loss is recoverable depends on the retained log, permission to read it, and sufficient resources to retrieve and use it. A test with the handle unavailable exposes a fallback requirement that a field-presence score would miss. Failing gracefully without acceptance can be the correct behavior when the required evidence cannot be reconstructed.

A context policy earns its operating point through this combination of measurements. Compare feasible policies by accepted outcomes, error categories, elapsed time, and total expenditure under the same task conditions. A shorter context with more unresolved trials is a trade-off to assess, not an automatic improvement. A structured record with high field retention but unsupported completion claims still fails the decision it was meant to support. No compression threshold or representation format supplies a universal winner.

::: {#chk-04-context-policy-evaluation .callout-checkpoint title="Testing what survives compaction"}

A policy preserves the manifest's field names but drops some values and version relationships. Its next request is shorter than the reference request.

- [ ] **Retention**: Can you define a check that distinguishes field presence from correct retention of the r18 reproducer result?
- [ ] **Evidence scope**: Which probe distinguishes a useful historical r17 failure from an unsupported claim about the current workspace?
- [ ] **Cost boundary**: If the model retrieves an omitted log on every subsequent turn, which measurements determine whether compaction saved resources?
- [ ] **Controlled comparison**: Why can a fixed-history probe diagnose a representation defect without establishing complete task performance?

:::

Evaluation turns a proposed context policy into a testable design. Its verdict remains bounded by the task fixtures, evidence criteria, and resource accounting used in the comparison. The recurring errors arise when one of those measurements is promoted into a stronger claim, such as treating short input as sufficient information or preserved text as enforced behavior.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-fallacies}

A compact request can omit a decisive assertion, and a complete transcript can preserve an obsolete file beside its replacement. These failures come from confusing the representation sent to the model with the information and controls the task requires.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *If every token fits, every needed fact is usable.*

The interface's capacity limit admits a request; it does not establish that the model will use its evidence adequately. Relevant details can be missing from a short request or difficult to distinguish in a long one. The capacity experiment must vary the information and layout as well as record length, then measure the required decision quality on the intended workload. A larger window removes one admission constraint without deciding which observations remain relevant or current.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Treating deterministic extraction as lossless task understanding.*

A parser can reproducibly retain the same error lines and omit the same decisive warning. Its deterministic behavior makes the transformation inspectable; it does not establish that the selection is sufficient. Preserve specified task-critical fields, label omissions, and retain access to original payloads where the task permits it. A handle helps only when the payload remains retrievable within the available access and resource limits.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *A valid progress-record schema guarantees continued compliance.*

A record can contain every required field while misreporting a check or omitting the version to which it applies. Even an accurate record can be followed by a proposal that violates a retained restriction. Validate the specified fields against their sources, evaluate subsequent behavior, and enforce action limits outside the prompt. Context preparation communicates the task's constraints; it does not supply the execution boundary.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Keeping obsolete support solely to preserve a prefix hit.*

Appending a notice leaves the old payload in the request and relies on the model to interpret their relationship. Removing or replacing the payload changes the token sequence and can reduce reuse from that point onward, but unchanged text is not worth preserving when it produces unsupported current-state claims. Choose the representation by its measured decision behavior and cost. A passing result remains a historical observation of its recorded version, not proof about every later version at the same path.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Placing unnecessary volatile fields before reusable content.*

A changing timestamp or request identifier can shorten the matching token prefix before otherwise stable task material. The layout calculation in \ref{nbk-04-quantitative-impact-of-prefix-layout} isolates the resulting input-charge difference under explicit reuse and pricing assumptions. The first differing token, not the message's role or the field's name, determines where exact-prefix matching ends. Move a field only when the new placement preserves the request's meaning, and do not infer a measured latency saving from the price calculation alone.

:::

The corrections preserve a common boundary. Working context presents selected information for a decision, while sources establish what was observed and runtime mechanisms enforce permitted effects. A policy is useful when it preserves those distinctions within the call budget, not when it makes the prompt look complete or stable at any cost.

## Summary {#sec-vol3-context-engineering-summary}

The repair manifest follows one decision through several transformations. Selection identifies what the next call needs; staging gives that material a bounded representation; compaction shortens it; and a structured progress record preserves the supported observations, hypotheses, and unresolved work needed to continue. Invalidation then revisits support affected by relevant changes. Evaluation tests whether the resulting request enables adequate decisions, including when a required payload cannot be recovered or a check no longer describes the current candidate.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Context is selected information for the next decision"}

* **Capacity does not establish adequacy**: The serialized request must fit while leaving output headroom, but the useful input depends on the task, model, and representation. Measure decision quality and resource use rather than infer sufficiency from the nominal window.
* **Layout changes reuse, not authority**: Stable prefixes can avoid repeated input work under compatible serving conditions. Message roles, provenance, and change rate describe different properties; arranging them well does not authorize an action or establish that an observation is true.
* **Compaction preserves specified needs, not everything**: Protect the exact fields required by the current task and check summaries against their support. Raw-payload handles provide conditional access to omitted material, not evidence that the next call already contains it.
* **Historical evidence needs current interpretation**: A test result remains an observation of the version and conditions tested. Relevant changes can remove its support for a present-state claim without erasing history, while unrelated changes need not invalidate every observation.
* **Evaluate decisions as well as representations**: Field retention, constraint compliance, current-evidence use, and accepted outcomes measure different properties. Count all policy costs and unsuccessful trials before deciding whether a smaller request improves the system.

:::

The manifest makes context a selected working set (principle \ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}) whose adequacy can be tested at a particular decision, rather than inferred from its size. Version-scoped observations apply the rule that authority stays with the source (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}) without discarding valid historical evidence. Together, these rules make context preparation accountable for what it supplies and explicit about what remains unresolved.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From selected tokens to physical attention state"}

The runtime has chosen the token sequence for the next call, but the serving system must decide whether to retain the attention state computed from earlier compatible prefixes. Holding that state can avoid repeated work; it also occupies capacity during tool waits and across competing requests. @Sec-vol3-kv-cache develops the storage, sharing, and retention decisions for this derived state. Those decisions can change execution cost without changing which observations belong in the logical working context.

:::
